passages.text: Peter woke much earlier than his daily custom, came in to us, woke us, and said, “Let Faustinus and Faustinianus, together with Clement and the members of the household, follow me, so that we may go to a sheltered place by the sea and baptize her where no one can watch.” We went to the shore, found a calm, clean place among some rocks, and he baptized her. We brothers withdrew for the women’s sake, together with a brother and some others, bathed, and then came back and took the women with us. Going in this way to a hidden place, we prayed. Then, because of the crowd, Peter sent the women ahead, directing them to go by another road to the lodging, and permitted only us among the men to accompany our mother and those same women. We went to the lodging and spoke with one another while waiting for him to come. After a considerable number of hours Peter arrived, broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it, and gave it first to our mother and then to us, her sons. Thus we dined with her and blessed God.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source has singular ἀδελφῷ after the plural brothers. An additional fellow member of the community may be intended; he is left unnamed rather than silently omitted or identified as Peter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἄρτον ἐπ’ εὐχαριστίᾳ κλάσας καὶ ἐπιθεὶς ἅλας
lexical_decisions.chosen: broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The thanksgiving and salt are both explicit. The text is not supplemented with wine or made an explicit identification of a later eucharistic rite.

passages.text: Then, seeing that the crowd had come in, Peter sat down, told us to sit beside him, and began by explaining why he had sent us ahead from the baptism and had himself arrived late. He gave the following reason: “As soon as you withdrew,” he said, “an old laborer came in with us, inquisitively concealing himself. Having watched us beforehand, as he later admitted, to see what we would do when we entered the sheltered place, he came out secretly and followed. At a suitable place he approached, greeted me, and said, ‘I have followed you for a long time, wanting to speak with you, but I was ashamed, lest you be angry at me for being inquisitive. Now, if you wish, I will tell you what seems true to me.’ I answered, ‘Tell us what you think is good, and we will welcome you, even if what is said is not actually good, since with a good intention you have wanted to say what seems good to you.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive use of “steal” means hiding or stealing along rather than theft of property. The note preserves the figurative wording’s furtiveness.
The object is the man, not necessarily an endorsement of the truth of his statement, as the following concession makes clear.

passages.text: “The old man began speaking in this way: ‘When I saw that you had bathed in the sea and withdrawn to the hidden place, I secretly approached and watched to see what you would do on entering a concealed place. When I saw you praying, I withdrew. Pitying you, however, I waited so that I might speak to you as you came out and persuade you not to be deceived. For there is neither God nor providence; everything is subject to destiny assigned at birth. I am fully convinced of this from what I have suffered, having studied the discipline carefully for a long time. So do not be deceived, child. Whether you pray or not, you are bound to suffer what comes from natal destiny. For if prayers or doing good had any power, I myself would be in better circumstances. Now, if this poor clothing of mine does not mislead you, you will not disbelieve what I say. Once, when I had great material abundance, I sacrificed much to the gods and provided much for the needy; yet, though I prayed and acted reverently, I could not escape what was fated.’ I said, ‘What have you suffered?’ He answered, ‘There is no need to speak of it now. Perhaps at the end you will hear who I am, whose family I belong to, and in what circumstances of life I have come to be. For now I want you to be fully convinced that everything is subject to natal destiny.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: destiny assigned at birth / natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένεσις literally refers to birth or origin; in this discussion it denotes fate inferred from a nativity or astrological birth configuration. The later explicit reference to astrology supports this contextual rendering, not a blanket substitution for every use of the word.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε γὰρ θεός ἐστιν οὔτε πρόνοια
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is neither God nor providence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is the old man’s stated position, not an assertion added by the narrator or translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίς τε ὢν ἐγὼ καὶ τίνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: who I am, whose family I belong to
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical plural genitive can concern ancestry or kin. It is not supplied as a particular named family.

passages.text: “I said, ‘If everything is subject to natal destiny and you are fully convinced that this is so, your advice reflects thoughts contrary to your own. For if even thinking cannot occur contrary to natal destiny, why do you labor in vain, advising that something happen which cannot happen? Moreover, even if natal destiny has existence, do not hurry to persuade me not to worship the master of the stars as well, at whose will even what is not to happen can happen. For what is subordinate must always obey its ruler. Worshiping the supposed gods, however, is superfluous if natal destiny prevails. For nothing happens contrary to what seems good to fate, nor can they themselves do anything, being subject to their universal natal destiny. If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself.’”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ θέλοντος καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι τι, γενέσθαι δυνατόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: at whose will even what is not to happen can happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the negated infinitive as characterizing an event not otherwise destined to happen; the final γενέσθαι then states that it can happen at the ruler’s will. This supplies the contextual relation to destiny in English, not a Greek emendation. Another possible linkage places μὴ γενέσθαι directly within what the ruler wills: “when he wills even that something not happen, its happening is possible.” That is more difficult in the argument, but the negation’s attachment is not uniquely established here. The main text does not omit either occurrence of “happen” or the negative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γένεσις ἐστιν, ἀντίκειται τὸ μὴ πρῶτον ἄρχειν. ὑποκεῖσθαι οὐ δύναται ὡς ἀγένητον ἑαυτοῦ πρεσβύτερον μηδὲν ἔχον
lexical_decisions.chosen: If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional is retained. The nearest named referent is natal destiny, read as the ungenerated principle hypothesized by fatalism. The neuter ἀγένητον can refer to an understood principle rather than agree directly with feminine γένεσις. A reference back to God or an ungenerated divine principle is also possible and would change which ruler is said to be unsubordinated. The pronoun “it” deliberately does not add a noun identifying the unexpressed subject uniquely.

passages.text: “As we were saying such things to one another, a large crowd gathered. Then, looking at the crowd, I said, ‘I and my people have inherited from our ancestors the worship of God and have a command not to attend to natal destiny—I mean the discipline of astrology. For this reason I have paid it no attention. Thus I am not experienced in astrology; I will explain the things in which I am experienced. Since I cannot refute natal destiny from the very science concerning natal destiny, I wish to demonstrate in another way that affairs are governed by providence, and that everyone will receive honor or punishment according to what he does. Whether now or later makes no difference to me, provided that everyone will certainly receive the consequences of what he has done. Here is the proof that natal destiny does not exist. If someone standing here lacks eyes, has a crippled hand, a lame foot, or some other bodily condition that has no possibility of returning to health and lies beyond every profession of healing—someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time—and I, by petitioning God, provide the healing, when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny: if this happens in this way, are not those who blaspheme the God who made everything doing wrong?’ The old man answered, ‘Is saying that everything is subject to natal destiny blasphemy?’ I answered, ‘Very much so. For if all people’s sins, acts of impiety, and licentious deeds come from stars, and the stars were appointed by God to do these things, so that they bring about every grievous thing, everyone’s sins are referred back to him who placed natal destiny in the stars.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source denotes a people or tribe; its proper name is not supplied in the English.
This can refer to every promise or claim of healing as well as a healing occupation. The main text keeps the claim that the condition lies beyond professed healing ability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε ἐκ γενέσεως κατόρθωσιν τὸ τοιοῦτο οὐδέποτε λαβεῖν ἠδυνήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hypothetical demonstration’s premise is retained as Peter’s argument. No actual present healing or empirical validation is asserted by the translation.
